questions.q: Define 'government budget' and state the fiscal year it covers in India.
questions.a: A government budget is an annual financial statement showing estimated government receipts and expenditures for a fiscal year. In India, the fiscal year runs from April 1 to March 31. A wrong answer (e.g., calendar year Jan-Dec) reveals confusion with the accounting year used by companies or other countries.

questions.q: Explain why the budget is divided into Revenue Budget and Capital Budget. What economic distinction does this division capture?
questions.a: The division separates current/recurring transactions (revenue) from asset-creating/liability-changing transactions (capital). Revenue items do not affect the government's asset-liability position; capital items do. A student who says "revenue is for short term, capital for long term" misses the precise accounting distinction: revenue expenditure neither creates assets nor reduces liabilities, while capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities.

questions.q: Classify each of the following into Revenue Receipt, Revenue Expenditure, Capital Receipt, or Capital Expenditure: (a) Corporate tax collection, (b) Interest payment on government bonds, (c) Disinvestment proceeds from PSU stake sale, (d) Construction of a new AIIMS hospital.
questions.a: (a) Corporate tax collection → Revenue Receipt (neither creates liability nor reduces asset). (b) Interest payment on bonds → Revenue Expenditure (recurring cost, no asset creation). (c) Disinvestment proceeds → Capital Receipt (reduces government assets/equity). (d) Construction of AIIMS → Capital Expenditure (creates physical asset). Misclassifying (c) as revenue receipt is a common error — students forget asset reduction.

questions.q: The government announces a scheme to provide free smartphones to students in government schools. Identify the budget objective this serves and explain whether it would appear in the Revenue Budget or Capital Budget.
questions.a: This serves the redistribution objective (reducing inequality in access to digital education). The expenditure is Revenue Expenditure because it does not create a durable asset for the government; it is a transfer in kind. A student placing it in Capital Budget because "smartphones are assets" confuses government asset creation with beneficiary asset receipt.

questions.q: "During high inflation, the government should increase capital expenditure on infrastructure to boost supply." Evaluate this statement using the stabilization objective of the budget.
questions.a: The statement is flawed. During high inflation, stabilization requires contractionary fiscal policy — reducing aggregate demand. Increasing capital expenditure would raise demand further, worsening inflation. Stabilization uses budget tools (tax rates, expenditure levels) to counter business cycles: expansionary in recession, contractionary in inflation. A student agreeing misses the demand-side impact of expenditure.

questions.q: Construct a mini-budget for a hypothetical state government with the following items (in ₹ crore): GST collection 50,000; Salaries 30,000; Interest payments 15,000; Market borrowings 20,000; Road construction 25,000; Disinvestment 5,000. Present it in the two-component format (Revenue Budget and Capital Budget) and state the revenue surplus/deficit.
questions.a: Revenue Budget: Receipts = GST 50,000 (Revenue Receipt). Expenditure = Salaries 30,000 + Interest 15,000 = 45,000 (Revenue Expenditure). Revenue Surplus = 5,000. Capital Budget: Receipts = Market borrowings 20,000 + Disinvestment 5,000 = 25,000 (Capital Receipts). Expenditure = Road construction 25,000 (Capital Expenditure). Capital Budget balanced. A student putting borrowings in Revenue Receipts or road construction in Revenue Expenditure fails the capital/revenue distinction.
